paragraphs: This paper asks how much deep image visualization depends on learned weights and how much comes from network architecture. It studies convolutional networks whose weights remain random and untrained, applying them to image reconstruction, texture synthesis, and artistic style transfer. The experiments examine whether these networks already provide useful image representations.

For reconstruction, the method starts from white noise and recovers images from representations in feature space. The authors report statistically higher reconstruction quality than the same method using trained networks with the same architecture. For texture synthesis, they use scaled correlations between representations across multiple layers and report results almost indistinguishable from natural textures and textures synthesized with a trained network.

The style-transfer experiments also produce images with high perceptual quality that compete with prior work using pretrained networks. Together, these findings support the usefulness of untrained architectures for the visualization tasks studied. The authors suggest that this could eventually help compare architectures without training, presenting that application as a possibility.
neurips-2016-a-powerful-generative-model.tldr: Random, untrained convolutional networks support strong reconstruction, texture synthesis, and style transfer results in the tasks studied.

paragraphs: Many learning objectives combine a finite collection of terms into one quantity to minimize. Empirical risk minimization is an example of this form. This paper introduces an optimization method for such finite sums, building on SAGA. Its central aim is to combine accelerated convergence with a procedure that remains simple to use.

The acceleration result applies when the objective is smooth and strongly convex. These conditions are part of the guarantee: the abstract does not claim the same accelerated rate for every finite-sum objective. The method has only one parameter, its step size, and the authors describe it as substantially simpler than other accelerated approaches for finite sums.

The method can also handle objectives whose individual terms are nonsmooth. That broadens its applicability to problems often addressed using operator splitting methods. The contribution therefore has two connected parts: a convergence improvement under the stated smoothness and convexity conditions, and a simple optimization approach that also extends to a wider class of objectives.
neurips-2016-a-simple-practical-accelera.tldr: A method built on SAGA offers accelerated convergence for smooth, strongly convex finite sums with only a step-size parameter.

paragraphs: Understanding a scene can involve identifying its individual objects, including how many there are, where they appear, and what they are. This paper presents an inference framework for image models that explicitly represent objects. A recurrent neural network attends to scene elements and processes them sequentially, making probabilistic inferences about the scene.

A central feature is that the model learns how many inference steps to take. This lets the inference process accommodate scenes containing different numbers of objects. The authors apply the framework both to partially specified two-dimensional models, expressed as variable-sized variational autoencoders, and to fully specified three-dimensional models based on probabilistic renderers.

The reported models learn to count, locate, and classify multiple objects without supervision. The paper demonstrates decomposition of three-dimensional images in a single neural-network forward pass at very high speed. It also reports accurate inference relative to supervised counterparts and improved generalization arising from the network structure. These findings connect explicit object reasoning with efficient learned inference.
neurips-2016-attend-infer-repeat-fast-sc.tldr: A recurrent attention model learns to infer objects and choose its own number of processing steps, enabling fast unsupervised scene understanding.

paragraphs: Recommendation depends on matching a user with an item at an appropriate time. The paper emphasizes that the hidden features describing users and items can change together as interactions occur. Fixed representations, or representations updated only within discrete time periods, can be ineffective at capturing the finer temporal structure of those interactions.

The proposed model represents user and item features as coevolving processes in continuous time. This makes their joint evolution part of the recommendation model itself. The modeling choice matters because changes on either side of an interaction can be relevant to predicting subsequent behavior, and the timing of those changes need not align with predefined epochs.

To estimate the parameters, the authors develop an efficient convex optimization algorithm with low-rank space-sharing constraints. Experiments across diverse real-world datasets show significant improvements in user behavior prediction over the state-of-the-art methods considered. The stated evidence supports modeling temporal coevolution as a useful ingredient in prediction, alongside an optimization procedure designed to make the model practical.
neurips-2016-coevolutionary-latent-featu.tldr: A continuous-time model of jointly evolving user and item features improves behavior prediction in experiments on diverse real-world datasets.

paragraphs: Learning structured predictors without supervision requires discovering hidden structure while estimating the model that describes it. The paper considers a two-layer conditional modeling approach related to conditional random field autoencoders. Existing work in this setting faces both nonconvex optimization and the computational burden of calculating normalization quantities during inference.

The authors develop a convex relaxation that jointly captures latent structure and estimates model parameters. The optimality claim belongs to this relaxed formulation. Bringing both tasks into one convex problem provides a way to address their interdependence while avoiding the nonconvex formulation identified in the earlier approach.

The paper also expands applicability by using maximum a posteriori inference, which asks for a most probable configuration and imposes a weaker inference requirement. It demonstrates the model on graph matching and linear-chain structures using total unimodularity. Experimental results are described as promising. The contribution combines a different optimization formulation with reduced inference demands and demonstrations on two distinct structured problems.
neurips-2016-convex-two-layer-modeling-w.tldr: A convex relaxation jointly learns latent structure and model parameters while reducing inference requirements to maximum a posteriori inference.

paragraphs: Generating corresponding images in two domains usually suggests training on examples that are already paired. This paper introduces Coupled Generative Adversarial Networks, or CoGAN, to learn from separate collections of images instead. Its objective is to produce related image pairs even though the training data contain no corresponding pairs across the two domains.

CoGAN contains two generative adversarial networks, with one responsible for each domain. A weight-sharing constraint couples the networks. Through that shared structure, the framework learns a joint image distribution from samples drawn separately from the two individual distributions. The coupling is therefore the key modeling ingredient that connects otherwise unpaired training collections.

The authors apply CoGAN to several paired-image generation tasks and report convincing corresponding images in each task. They also demonstrate domain adaptation and cross-domain image generation applications. These results show how shared network weights can support learning cross-domain relationships without paired examples, broadening the training settings available for the demonstrated generative tasks.
neurips-2016-coupled-generative-adversar.tldr: CoGAN uses weight sharing between two adversarial networks to generate corresponding images from training collections that contain no paired examples.

paragraphs: Representative examples can help people understand a complex dataset, but they may leave important aspects of its distribution unexplained. This paper argues that an explanation should also include criticism: examples that reveal what the selected prototypes fail to capture. The aim is to help users build a more complete mental model of the data.

The authors introduce MMD-critic, an efficient method for selecting both prototypes and criticisms. Its motivation comes from Bayesian model criticism, applied here to the adequacy of an example-based explanation. Prototypes convey representative patterns, while criticisms draw attention to gaps in that representation. Their usefulness comes from these complementary roles.

A pilot study with human participants finds that the selected prototypes and criticisms help understanding and reasoning. The authors also evaluate the prototypes through a nearest-prototype classifier, reporting competitive performance against baselines. These evaluations address different aspects of the method: whether the examples assist people and whether the prototypes provide a useful representation for classification.
neurips-2016-examples-are-not-enough-lea.tldr: MMD-critic pairs representative examples with criticisms that expose their gaps, helping human understanding in a pilot study.

paragraphs: The stochastic block model describes networks whose nodes belong to communities, with connection probabilities determined by community membership. This paper studies when those communities can be recovered exactly. Its focus is a general setting in which community sizes, community counts, and connection patterns can differ substantially across the same network.

The model allows unrestricted numbers and sizes of communities, including different ways these quantities can grow with the number of nodes. It also permits general connection probabilities within and between communities. Within this setting, the authors establish exact-recovery guarantees for a semidefinite program and derive upper and lower bounds on model parameters governing recoverability.

The results account for tradeoffs among the parameters rather than considering each source of heterogeneity in isolation. This yields recovery guarantees for many additional model configurations. Allowing a broad model family does not mean every configuration is recoverable; the bounds characterize conditions relevant to that question. The contribution expands understanding of recovery in networks with uneven community structure.
neurips-2016-exploiting-tradeoffs-for-ex.tldr: Recovery bounds exploit tradeoffs among community sizes and connection probabilities in general heterogeneous stochastic block models.

paragraphs: Ordinal embedding places items in a low-dimensional space using comparisons about which items are closer together. Such comparisons often come from people and can contain errors. This paper studies independently corrupted judgments, where a correct comparison is reversed with some probability, and asks when a meaningful underlying arrangement can still be learned.

Under a generative data model, the authors derive bounds on how accurately a learned embedding predicts new comparisons. Their analysis uses the fact that the distance matrix for points in d dimensions has rank at most d plus two. This connects the low-dimensional representation to guarantees about predictions from a finite collection of noisy judgments.

The paper also shows that the underlying embedding can be recovered through a simple convex optimization problem. The argument addresses a key obstacle: the linear map describing comparisons is not invertible, although an invertible nonlinear map exists. Two new algorithms are proposed and experimentally evaluated. The results distinguish predicting unseen comparisons from recovering the underlying representation, providing theoretical support for both under the model.
neurips-2016-finite-sample-prediction-an.tldr: Under a generative model, noisy distance comparisons support bounded prediction error and recovery of an embedding through convex optimization.

paragraphs: Follow the leader chooses a decision based on what has performed best on previous losses. It is a simple online learning method, and curved loss functions are known to support good performance. This paper asks which other favorable conditions can produce small regret, focusing on linear prediction over a nonempty, convex, compact domain.

The authors show that curvature in the boundary of the allowed decision set can play a role similar to curvature in the losses. In this setting, follow the leader has logarithmic regret growth provided the lengths of the mean loss vectors stay bounded away from zero. The geometric property and the condition on the loss vectors both matter to this result.

The paper also gives finite expected regret results for polyhedral domains with stochastic data. Building on an existing meta-algorithm, it obtains a method that combines worst-case guarantees with the available follow-the-leader bound. These findings identify circumstances in which a simple procedure enjoys especially favorable performance while also supporting an algorithm with broader protection.
neurips-2016-following-the-leader-and-fa.tldr: Follow the leader can achieve fast regret rates through favorable domain geometry and data conditions, even with linear losses.

paragraphs: Sparse-Group Lasso is a linear regression method that encourages sparsity at two levels: individual features and groups of features. This is useful when variables have a meaningful group structure and the desired solution should select among both groups and their members. Computing that solution can still be demanding in high-dimensional problems.

The paper introduces provably safe screening rules that identify features or groups that will be inactive in the optimal solution. A solver can discard these components early, reducing the amount of work remaining. Safety is the crucial property: the screening rules certify inactivity at the optimum, making early removal compatible with solving the original optimization problem.

The rules rely on efficient dual-gap calculations using geometric properties of the epsilon-norm. The authors incorporate them into a coordinate descent implementation and report significant reductions in computing time. The contribution therefore improves how Sparse-Group Lasso is solved by using mathematical certificates to eliminate unnecessary computation while retaining its feature-level and group-level selection behavior.
neurips-2016-gap-safe-screening-rules-fo.tldr: Provably safe screening removes inactive features and groups early, substantially accelerating the authors’ Sparse-Group Lasso solver.

paragraphs: Cooperative tasks can require several agents to coordinate their actions through communication. Often, the rules for exchanging information are manually specified and remain fixed during training. This paper investigates whether agents can instead learn how to communicate as part of learning how to act, using a simple neural model called CommNet.

CommNet uses continuous communication among multiple agents in fully cooperative tasks. The communication mechanism is learned alongside the agents’ policy. This ties the development of messages to the behavior needed for the shared task, making communication part of the learning problem rather than a separately prescribed protocol.

Across a diverse set of tasks, the authors find that agents learn to communicate and improve performance over agents without communication and other baselines. In some cases, the learned language can be interpreted, revealing simple strategies that help solve the task. This interpretability claim is qualified: it applies to some cases. The broader empirical finding is that jointly learning communication and behavior can improve cooperation.
neurips-2016-learning-multiagent-communi.tldr: CommNet learns continuous communication alongside cooperative policies, improving performance across tasks and sometimes revealing interpretable strategies.

paragraphs: Learning algorithms often behave differently when the magnitude of their target signal changes. In value-based reinforcement learning, this matters because appropriate value estimates can change scale as the agent’s behavior policy changes. The paper proposes adaptive normalization of the targets used in learning updates to address this moving scale.

The motivating application is learning to play Atari games with one algorithm. Earlier work clipped rewards to a fixed range, making learning across games easier. However, clipping changes the reward function and can produce qualitatively different behavior. The issue therefore concerns both the numerical scale encountered during learning and the behavior encouraged by the resulting rewards.

Adaptive normalization allows the authors to remove this domain-specific clipping heuristic without reducing overall performance. The finding supports adjusting the scale of learning targets as an alternative way to accommodate varying signal magnitudes in the studied setting. The reported outcome concerns overall performance; it does not assert an improvement on every individual game.
neurips-2016-learning-values-across-many.tldr: Adaptive target normalization removes reward clipping in the studied reinforcement learning setting without reducing overall performance.

paragraphs: Deep image embeddings represent images as points whose distances express similarity. Training often emphasizes difficult examples selected using Euclidean distance. This paper argues that a single global distance can be misleading in a complex feature space: same-class examples in a dense region may be farther apart than different-class examples in a sparse region.

The proposed Position-Dependent Deep Metric unit learns a similarity measure that adapts to local feature structure. It uses this measure to identify difficult examples within local neighborhoods and guide embedding learning online. The unit can be inserted into convolutional networks and trained end to end, connecting local similarity estimation directly to representation learning.

The authors report faster convergence and improved performance on two challenging image retrieval datasets. They also report stronger generalization in large and open-set transfer-learning and zero-shot settings on ImageNet 2010 and ImageNet-10K, linking this behavior to the method’s large-margin nature. The findings support taking local feature structure into account when deciding which training examples are difficult.
neurips-2016-local-similarity-aware-deep.tldr: A learned, position-dependent similarity metric improves hard-example selection, convergence, and generalization in the reported image embedding experiments.

paragraphs: Maximum Mean Discrepancy, or MMD, measures distance between probability distributions by representing them in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space. Applications generally have finite samples rather than direct access to the distributions. This paper asks how accurately MMD can be estimated from those samples and whether commonly used estimators already achieve the best possible rate.

The authors derive lower bounds on estimation error for any radial universal kernel on Euclidean space. Lower bounds describe a fundamental limit on estimation accuracy. Their bounds match existing upper bounds apart from constants that depend only on properties of the kernel, connecting achievable performance with the difficulty inherent in the estimation problem.

This establishes minimax rate optimality for the empirical estimator and its U-statistic variant. In plain terms, these familiar estimators achieve the best worst-case rate under the setting studied. Rate optimality concerns how estimation accuracy scales with sample size; the remaining kernel-dependent constants are still part of the comparison. The result provides theoretical support for estimators already used in applications.
neurips-2016-minimax-estimation-of-maxim.tldr: Matching lower and upper bounds establish minimax rate optimality of common MMD estimators for radial universal kernels.

paragraphs: A system that repeatedly places items in a list must learn from feedback while deciding what to display next. The difficulty is that an item may receive no useful feedback because the user ignored it. Without accounting for this, the system faces ambiguity about what observed behavior says about the item itself.

The paper studies this problem in a multiple-play semi-bandit setting using the Position-based click model. It proposes exploiting available information about how display position biases user attention. The authors also explain how this model differs from the Cascade model and its variants, making the feedback assumptions central to the learning problem.

The theoretical contribution includes a new regret lower bound for the position-based model, characterizing limits on sequential learning performance. The authors also provide computationally efficient algorithms with favorable theoretical and empirical results. Together, these contributions address both what performance is fundamentally attainable under this click model and how to learn effectively when displayed content may go unnoticed.
neurips-2016-multiple-play-bandits-in-th.tldr: Position-aware bandit algorithms use known display bias to learn from ambiguous click feedback, with new regret bounds and favorable empirical results.

paragraphs: Online convex optimization involves making decisions while loss functions are revealed over time. This paper introduces RescaledExp for an unconstrained setting in which no bounds on the loss functions are known in advance. Its objective is to provide strong regret guarantees without requiring that prior information or hyperparameter tuning.

A central theoretical result identifies the cost of not knowing a loss bound. The authors prove an exponential separation between the regret available to existing methods that require such knowledge and what can be achieved by algorithms without it. RescaledExp asymptotically matches the resulting lower bound as the number of iterations grows, establishing optimality in the setting it addresses.

The algorithm is naturally hyperparameter-free. Empirical results show that it matches earlier optimization algorithms that require hyperparameter optimization. The theory and experiments offer complementary findings: the lower bound explains the unavoidable difficulty of operating without advance bounds, while the experiments demonstrate competitive performance without the tuning required by the comparison methods.
neurips-2016-online-convex-optimization-.tldr: RescaledExp achieves asymptotically optimal regret without advance loss bounds and empirically matches methods requiring hyperparameter tuning.

paragraphs: Random Fourier Features approximate kernels using randomized feature representations. This paper finds that the choice of random transformation has an important effect on approximation quality. Replacing a Gaussian random matrix with a properly scaled random orthogonal matrix substantially reduces kernel approximation error. The authors call this approach Orthogonal Random Features, or ORF.

The paper supports ORF with both theoretical analysis and experiments. It then introduces Structured Orthogonal Random Features, or SORF, to reduce the cost of applying the transformation. SORF uses structured discrete orthogonal matrices, reducing computation from quadratic in the data dimension to the dimension multiplied by its logarithm.

The authors report that this speed improvement comes with almost no loss of kernel approximation quality relative to ORF. Experiments on several datasets support the effectiveness of both methods compared with existing approaches. The contribution links more accurate random feature construction with faster computation, and the paper also discusses potential uses of the discrete orthogonal structure for other kernels and applications.
neurips-2016-orthogonal-random-features-.tldr: Orthogonal random transformations improve kernel approximation, while a structured version accelerates computation with almost no loss of approximation quality.

paragraphs: Region-based object detectors can spend substantial computation repeatedly processing candidate regions from the same image. R-FCN addresses this cost with a fully convolutional design that shares almost all computation across the image. The goal is to preserve accurate detection while reducing expensive work repeated separately for each region.

The central mechanism is a set of position-sensitive score maps. These address a tension between image classification, which benefits from recognizing an object despite changes in location, and detection, which must retain information about location. This design allows fully convolutional classification backbones, including Residual Networks, to be used naturally for object detection.

With a 101-layer ResNet, the paper reports competitive PASCAL VOC results, including 83.6% mean average precision on the 2007 dataset. It reports a test time of 170 milliseconds per image and speeds 2.5 to 20 times faster than the Faster R-CNN counterpart. These findings demonstrate the practical benefit of sharing computation while retaining position-sensitive information for detection.
neurips-2016-r-fcn-object-detection-via-.tldr: R-FCN shares nearly all image computation and uses position-sensitive score maps to deliver competitive detection accuracy with substantially faster testing.

paragraphs: Active learning usually gives a learner access to a labeling oracle: it can ask for the label of an example. This paper considers a second kind of assistance, called SEARCH. SEARCH represents a human looking through a database to find an example that can seed a solution or serve as a counterexample to an existing one.

The distinction concerns what the human is asked to contribute. Labeling supplies information about an example already selected for a query. Searching can identify a relevant example in response to the current solution. The authors treat SEARCH as a stronger oracle and argue that this form of assistance is natural to implement in many situations.

The main result shows that an algorithm using both LABEL and SEARCH can obtain exponentially large improvements over using LABEL alone. These gains depend on the problem; they are not claimed for every active learning setting. The finding makes the design of human assistance itself consequential: changing the available query types can substantially change what a learner can achieve.
neurips-2016-search-improves-label-for-a.tldr: Combining labeling with human search for useful examples can yield exponentially large, problem-dependent improvements in active learning.

paragraphs: Structured prediction involves outputs with related components, making the structure of a predictor relevant to its learning guarantees. This paper develops data-dependent margin bounds for broad families of losses and hypotheses with arbitrary factor graph decompositions. The authors describe these as the tightest known margin bounds for both multiclass and general structured prediction problems.

The guarantees use a measure called factor graph complexity together with a measure of feature and graph sparsity. Factor graph complexity can be estimated from data and related to familiar quantities for several common hypothesis classes. This gives the analysis a way to account for the data and the predictor’s structural organization.

The authors extend the theory using Voted Risk Minimization, obtaining learning guarantees even with complex factor graphs. They derive two algorithms, Voted Conditional Random Field and Voted Structured Boosting, that can use complex features and graphs while retaining favorable guarantees. Experiments with the former on several datasets provide empirical validation. The proof techniques also include generalizations of Talagrand’s contraction lemma.
neurips-2016-structured-prediction-theor.tldr: Factor graph complexity yields data-dependent structured prediction guarantees and motivates two algorithms that accommodate complex features and graphs.

paragraphs: Newton-type optimization uses curvature information, but assembling that information can be expensive when an objective contains many terms. This paper studies convex objectives formed from a sum plus a regularizer, focusing on the regime where the number of terms greatly exceeds the dimension. It assumes low-rank factorizations of the individual Hessians are readily available.

The proposed algorithms reduce computation by sampling Hessian contributions nonuniformly and allowing inexact updates. Two sampling distributions are considered, based on block norm squares and block partial leverage scores. The approach makes the selection of curvature contributions a central part of designing a cheaper Newton-type method.

Under stated assumptions, the algorithms retain a linear-quadratic convergence rate and have lower computational complexity than similar existing methods. The authors also report greater robustness and improved dependence on problem-specific quantities such as the condition number. Numerical experiments on several real datasets demonstrate advantages. The contribution combines conditional convergence guarantees with computational savings tailored to the structure of large finite-sum problems.
neurips-2016-sub-sampled-newton-methods-.tldr: Nonuniform Hessian sampling and inexact updates reduce Newton-method costs while preserving linear-quadratic convergence under stated assumptions.

paragraphs: Tensor networks provide efficient approximations of high-order tensors and have been useful in physics and mathematics. This paper brings that representation machinery into supervised learning. It investigates how existing algorithms for optimizing tensor networks can be adapted to train predictive models from labeled data.

The authors use matrix product states, also called tensor trains, to parameterize nonlinear kernel learning models. The tensor network supplies an organized representation of the model’s parameters, drawing on the efficiency of working with these tensor approximations. The contribution connects a particular model representation with optimization methods developed for that representation, giving tensor networks a concrete role in supervised prediction.

On MNIST, the resulting approach achieves a test-set classification error below one percent. This provides an empirical demonstration that the adapted methods can support accurate classification on the dataset studied. The paper also discusses how to interpret the additional structure that the tensor network imposes on the learned model, addressing the character of the representation as well as its predictive performance.
neurips-2016-supervised-learning-with-te.tldr: Tensor-network optimization is adapted to nonlinear kernel learning, achieving below one percent test classification error on MNIST.

paragraphs: Sparse graphical modeling seeks to identify conditional relationships among variables. A neighborhood-selection approach models each variable’s conditional mean using a sparse function of the others. The Multiple Quantile Graphical Model extends this idea by modeling several conditional quantiles, describing multiple parts of the conditional distribution instead of only its mean.

This gives the model a richer way to represent distributions whose variability changes with other variables or whose shape is non-Gaussian. Under suitable regularity conditions, the authors prove that the probability of identifying the exact conditional independencies tends to one as problem size grows. The guarantee extends beyond the usual constant-variance Gaussian setting while retaining explicit conditions.

The paper provides an efficient fitting algorithm based on the alternating direction method of multipliers. It also describes how to sample from the joint distribution underlying the estimate. Experiments demonstrate flexibility and effectiveness on heteroskedastic, non-Gaussian data. Together, the theory, fitting procedure, and sampling strategy support a broader approach to estimating sparse conditional relationships.
neurips-2016-the-multiple-quantile-graph.tldr: Modeling multiple conditional quantiles enables richer sparse graphical models, with conditional-independence recovery guarantees under suitable regularity conditions.

paragraphs: Social dynamics connects interactions between individuals with changes across a population. This paper focuses on predicting individual state changes, such as infection or opinion transitions, using information about those interactions. Its objective is efficient inference about particular people within a large evolving system.

The authors introduce a stochastic kinetic model to capture adaptive transition probabilities. They pair it with a variational inference algorithm whose complexity grows linearly with the number of individuals rather than exponentially. This scaling property is central to handling dynamic interactions across large populations while retaining predictions at the individual level.

The method is evaluated through epidemic-dynamics experiments using wireless sensor network data collected from more than ten thousand people over three years. The algorithm tracks disease transmission and predicts each individual’s infection probability. The authors report greater efficiency than sampling while maintaining high accuracy. These results support using an interaction-based model with approximate inference to make detailed predictions at a scale where computational demands are a central concern.
neurips-2016-using-social-dynamics-to-ma.tldr: A stochastic kinetic model with linearly scaling variational inference predicts individual infection risk efficiently in large-population experiments.
